What does not come along is the “ought”, and it has two parts that do different work. Calling widening better is C, the only premise of the ethics that orders. Counting the futures that never return to oneself is scope, not order: it is the condition's step of invariance (section 6.11), which fixes whose possibilities count and ranks nothing (section 6.15). Both are open questions of warrant (section 8.5), and neither is a premise of any law here.

**What widening counts.** `Web.Widens` compares which members of the world's type of formations `F`, given in advance, the levels admit at the thresholds the web fixes (`Web.Admits`; requirements as thresholds, section 0, block A). A course that brings about a kind of formation or a requirement outside `F` widens nothing on this measure, so 生生, read as creating the conditions and generators of further forming (D1), can exceed what widening registers. Widening over a world that grows, along the growth by attachment of `Flow.GrownBy` (`Becoming.Cuts`), is open (section 8.1, item 5).

- **Calling the generative space good.** After the reduction to possibilities, the content of calling it good is the condition's step of invariance (§6.11). That widening is better is a question of warrant, not a premise of any law (§6.13): C's no-loss extension is exactly widening by definition, so the definition carries no warrant.

- **Calling the generative space good.** Two questions of warrant, which do different work:
  - *Is widening better?* The warrant of C, the only premise of the ethics that orders. C's no-loss extension is exactly widening by definition (§6.13), so the definition carries no warrant.
  - *Does significance stop at no boundary?* The warrant of the condition's step of invariance (§6.11), which fixes scope, whose losses count, and orders nothing.
